但我觉得真正有意思的不是“AI 让开发变快了”，而是他们在产品上做了几件挺反直觉的事情

第一，干脆重新做了一个产品

他们没有继续往原来的 AI 产品里塞 Agent Tab。Roman 有句话挺好：不断加入口、加 Tab，很容易变成 “shipping your org chart”
，把公司内部的组织结构直接做进产品里

用户最后看到的是几个互不相干的产品理念被硬塞进同一个界面

所以他们选择从零开始，先问一个问题：

如果未来工作真的变成“把事情交给一群 AI 同事”，这个产品应该长什么样？

第二，前 200–300 个用户，团队一个个手动 onboard

不是发个邀请码、看数据，而是核心团队自己坐进去做二十分钟的 onboarding call

电脑启动慢了、用户不知道下一步干什么、某个流程卡住了，第二天直接修

甚至刻意去找咖啡店老板这种完全不在硅谷 AI 圈的人，因为内部员工和 AI power user 太容易形成认知盲区

这个我很喜欢，而且这个也比较重要，如果没有类似的外部信息，项目很容易走偏

AI 产品变化太快，现在很多时候定量数据甚至还没积累出意义，最快的学习方式反而重新变成了最原始的：

坐在用户旁边看他怎么用

第三，也是我觉得最重要的：

他们把 Grok Bot 当“同事”，而不是“工具”

这直接影响了一堆产品设计

比如他们会主动隐藏大量模型内部过程、tool call、点击动作

原因很简单：

你把一件事交给同事，不会要求他每点击一次网页都汇报给你

Agent 也是一样

现在很多 Agent 产品喜欢疯狂展示：
正在搜索……
正在调用……
正在思考……
正在点击……

某种程度上还是在用“软件工具”的思路做 Agent。这个我非常同意，当前的AI 产品都太“工程师”了

Grok Bot 的判断是，模型越可靠，这些东西反而越应该消失

用户真正想知道的是：

事情做完了吗？
结果怎么样？
什么时候需要我介入？

第四，每个 Bot 有自己的 cloud computer

不是远程控制你的电脑，而是它自己拥有一台可以持续工作的电脑

这件事情会让 Agent 从“帮我操作”变成真正的异步 worker

甚至他们内部自然出现了一个很有意思的玩法：

有人把自己最信任的 Bot 提升成 “Chief of Staff”，再让它去给其他 Bot 分发任务

这个产品形态不是团队提前设计出来的，而是用户自己长出来的

第五，上线前最重要的工作之一不是 shipping，而是 unshipping

他们删掉了大量实验功能、developer-style observability 和复杂 UI

Roman 还提到一个产品判断方式：

不要问：

“Grok Bot now has X.”

而要问：

“Grok Bot can now do X.”

前者很容易让团队不停堆功能

后者逼着你思考：用户到底因此多完成了什么事情？

我看完最大的感受是：

Agent 产品可能正在经历一次很根本的产品范式变化

过去软件追求的是：

让用户更高效地完成工作

Copilot 是：

和用户一起完成工作。

真正的 Agent 则是：

用户把工作交出去

所以 Roman 有句话我觉得特别重要：

一个 AI 帮你完成 90% 的工作，和真正完成 100%，不是 10% 的差距，而是两种完全不同的产品

因为前者你仍然要监督它，后者你开始信任它

Agent 下一阶段真正竞争的，可能不是谁能接更多 MCP、调用更多工具

而是谁最先让用户产生这种感觉：

“这件事我交给它就行了。”

Watching an AI log into a remote cloud desktop, click around on my behalf, and get stuck in endless 2FA loops made me realize how fake our security actually is. We’re forcing super-smart AI agents to wear human masks just to get basic tasks done online.

We desperately need a shift to actual cryptographic proof:

* Hardware keys instead of text message codes
* Cryptographic delegation instead of handing over my passwords
* Real proof of work behind the scenes instead of manual friction

quote:
OpenClaw walked so Grok Bot and Muse could run

Around January 2026, @OpenClaw suddenly seemed to be everywhere…

It showed the world what happens when AI stops being only a chatbot you ask questions and becomes an agent that actually does work for you.

A few weeks later, I bought a Mac Mini and started building Sara, my personal AI agent, and sharing that journey online.

Sara still runs mostly on OpenClaw today, and I still love it… I love that it is open source. I love being able to run it locally, inspect everything, change how it works, connect random tools, break things, fix them, and learn in the process.

But if I’m honest, the product experience is not delightful enough for a general audience.

Most people will never open Terminal to run ‘openclaw update’ or ‘openclaw doctor --fix’. They do not want to manage a Mac Mini, API keys, configuration files, permissions, models, and all the small things that make an always-on agent work.

And they shouldn’t have to…

Grok Bot @bot by @xAI, and now Muse by @Meta announced today, feel like productized versions of the same big idea for a much wider audience.

The setup is simple. Your agent gets a virtual computer out of the box (no Mac Mini required). Connecting tools, setting permissions, and keeping everything running feels like part of the product instead of a technical project.

That may sound like packaging, but great packaging is what brings technology to everyone.

From my first day using OpenClaw, the direction felt clear to me: eventually, we will all have personal agents doing real work for us. At work, but also across our personal lives. Planning, researching, buying, organizing, remembering, following up, and quietly getting things done while we sleep.

Sara is that agent for me.

I think OpenClaw will continue to have a big place in this future. There is real value in an open-source option you can run locally, fully control, and shape however you want. For builders and people who like to tinker, that freedom matters a lot.

But like most software, I expect the majority of people will choose the packaged, hosted version. Less control, but far less work to manage and maintain.

OpenClaw gave builders an early look at this future and inspired others to stand on its shoulders. Grok Bot and Muse may bring that future to everyone else.

It looks like many more people are about to get their own Sara.

quote:
I'm still bullish on Grok Bot over Instinct and the new Muse AI assistant.

Skills are Grok Bot’s quiet moat. Grok Bot treats workflows as durable objects. Skill is a reusable recipe: when to use it, the steps, the decision rules, the expected output, the boundaries. You can write one. You can correct one. Or you can Teach a task, like screen-record the workflow on the Bot’s computer and it drafts the skill from the demonstration.

Chat memory, on the other hand, is trapped in one conversation. Skills are shared across every Bot you run. So the scheduling playbook you taught once does not live in “that one helpful thread.” It becomes infrastructure. Another Bot can invoke it. A routine can point at it. A template can package the whole job, including instructions, skills, routines, and someone else can install it.

Instinct and peers are still mostly: smarter reply in a box. Grok Bot is: show the work once, keep the operating system.

This is the same movie Cursor already played in code. Accept/reject on real diffs became training signal. The Cursor team is applying this moat yet again to personal agents.

The industry keeps waiting for a model leap to make agents useful. Skills are the opposite bet: make the workflow compound, and the same intelligence stops stalling.

quote:
???
“Mostly true” as a workflow, overstated as an official “Grok engineer just dropped this” product.0
The post itself is real. @gippp69 is describing a file-based self-improvement pattern and pairing it with a 24-second video of a one-pager titled How to build self-improving agents with Grok. That graphic matches the earlier summary: two loops, compact knowledge files, six writing principles, five design questions.0
What is actually true
The idea is a real and useful agent-engineering pattern:
•One loop does the work (task → observe → act → human review).
•Another loop reviews outcomes later and writes small reusable lessons.
•Those lessons live in short markdown/knowledge files instead of one ever-growing prompt.
•Later runs read those files, so useful patterns compound without fine-tuning the model.
That matches how Grok Build is actually designed to be customized:
•Persistent files such as AGENTS.md and MEMORY.md
•Skills as reusable markdown packages
•Lifecycle hooks
•/dream memory consolidation (experimental, off by default)
•/loop for scheduled prompts
•Subagents and review/verify loops inside /goal48
Community projects go further in the same direction (persistent lesson files, perpetual loops, observational memory). So the post is describing something people can and do build on Grok’s stack. It is not inventing a fake capability.1
What is not cleanly true
“A Grok engineer just showed this” is the weak part. I could not find an official xAI/SpaceXAI guide that matches this exact two-loop one-pager, those six principles, or those marketing stats. It reads like a polished community synthesis styled to look official. The same account’s quoted X article is a different guide (a repo-ops desk), not this self-improvement poster.20
The numbers on the graphic (250K+ developers, 72% faster iteration) are not corroborated in official docs I found. Treat them as promotional.
This is also not model-level recursive self-improvement. The weights do not update. The system gets better because you persist distilled lessons in files and force later runs to read them. Bad lessons can still compound if there is no human gate — which the graphic itself flags.
Bottom line
•The post’s description of the method is accurate.
•The method is real and workable on Grok Build / Grok Bot if you implement the files, hooks, and review loop.
•The “official Grok engineer reveal” framing is not independently verified.
•Expect improvement in repeatable workflow quality, not a suddenly smarter base model.
If you want, I can turn that poster into a concrete file layout (MEMORY.md, lesson files, hook + /loop schedule) you can drop into a Grok Build repo.

Here is my experience setting up @TownAI , Instinct @noahrshinn , and Muse, all at roughly the same time.

Town has a great setup and walks you through the whole thing very smoothly. It's also very powerful, and you can communicate with it through the app, through different messaging apps, through email. It's very powerful, and you can interface with it in a lot of ways.

With that said, when I try to multitask through WhatsApp on Town, it drops the ball a lot. Also, you blow through credits fast on this thing. I would call Town high-end, but expensive. If I were to use it as my daily driver, I would not only need the $200/month plan, I'd probably have to be buying extra credits.

Instinct is getting hyped a lot right now by people trying to make money off it, IMO. At first, it doesn't feel as powerful as something like Town, but the more I use it, the more I like it. I'm on Android, so I only communicate with it through WhatsApp. For the time being, it's free, and there is no paid version. It has a lot of horsepower behind it. They must be spending a boatload on tokens right now, and that can't last forever without charging customers.

On one level, Instinct doesn't feel as powerful and multidimensional as Town, but on another level, its simplicity and elegance is really nice. I like how casual it feels, and it's deceptively powerful.

Muse has an incredible amount of horsepower behind it. I gave it two very intensive tasks, and it moved through them very quickly. Also, integrations are really smooth. It learns super fast, and you can throw a lot at it. They must be using a lot of compute on this right now, and it's a good value for the money right now, meaning there's a free plan and if you want to upgrade, there's a $20/month plan and a $100/month plan. My sense is it's a better value than Town, at least right now, but all of that can change in the future.

I want to give an honorable mention to @TaskletAI . I see it in a very similar way to Town, just not as dressed up and polished, but their $25/month plan is a pretty good value, especially if you use Luna with it. You can get a lot done at a low cost.

There seems to be a frantic race to see who's going to be the AI agent of choice. My personal favorite is still Hermes @NousResearch and I also have a ChatGPT Pro and @perplexity_ai Max plan. quote:
My way too early takes on Meta Muse, their foray into the personal AI agent arena

First impressions:

- its very fast and snappy, a nice change from the time you need to spend watching a prompt go through with other products. The product of good model routing? Use a fast/cheap one for the basics, bump up to heavy duty for the computer use?

- not iMessage based (although you can connect WhatsApp), the app is pretty good and offers much more user interaction points than just a long chat. Ideas for prompts, automations, and use cases are prominently displayed, making it easier for a casual user to get started. Ability to have multiple chats is nice. I maintain that iMessage will just be a channel and the long term goal of all personal agents is to have some first class app interface

- payments, security, controls, are front and center. Partnership with Stripe to use Link to check out

- secrets/credentials handling is very smooth, it's nice to just have a place to see everything connected in the app

- payment protections (refunds) for agents is something no one has offered to date, although it's been much debated, will be interesting to see if it drives increased agentic commerce as people trust the agent more

- have yet to do anything heavy duty on it with computer use, so can't say how it compares on that front to Instinct or Grok Bot. As a lightweight assistant, it seems good enough already. Computer use was one of the biggest differentiators for this past wave of assistants so will need to dig in more there. Success rates here will be a big thing to watch

- responses, while very fast, feel a bit more mechanical and not as smart. Tradeoffs! This is probably just the difference between Muse Spark and whatever Instinct runs

- One thing Instinct is particularly good at is being proactive without being pushy - haven't had Muse long enough to know how it does on that front

- Onboarding, not as smooth and premium as Instinct - which makes sense if you think of Instinct as more as premium software and Muse as something for everyone

- Meta having their own models combined with massive amounts of available compute + hardware they own will be a big moat and edge at scale. They can serve results faster, have less downtime, and keep success rates higher

- If they can execute, this can be a very valuable product for Meta and potentially the big consumer AI breakthrough they've been looking for. It may not be perfect for the VC/startup power user that prefers Instinct but it can be good enough for the billions of other people that already use Meta apps. Auto-distribution can make it a Threads level success. Meta ultimately just wants to keep people sticky to their properties and if you end up paying for additional usage, it's a bonus. Just integrating this natively into WhatsApp would be a massive product. This is all a funnel to drive use of Muse Spark

- Pressure may actually be on ChatGPT the most as the preeminent consumer AI product - I get the sense you can get way more out of the free tier of Muse than you can the free levels of ChatGPT. This might be a Trojan Horse for Meta to gain mass adoption for their models. I think Muse is massively subsidized, I have not made a dent on the usage yet. So if you're just a user of ChatGPT, maybe you just come and use Muse instead and get sticky with the personal assistant experience.

quote:
The screen said +203 SOL. The PUMP button was green. Chief of Memecoins sat in the middle like a DJ. Pixel figures ran underneath: SNIPER, SCAN, WHALE, SEARCH, RUG, SHILL, EXIT, RISK. Up top, “rugs dodged.” The clip looks like a casino congratulating itself.

I did not get rich off that button. I almost sat on it with my whole chest.

The first week I did not build a desk with Grok Bot. I built an arcade. Sniper watches a pair. Scan yells “new pair found.” Whale pumps volume. Shill writes a thread. Rug scanner paints bars. Risk whispers “cut the tail.” All of it on one shared machine, one notebook, and one fantasy: if the lines are green, I must be smart.

The first “quiet” night was not quiet. The desk caught volume. Sniper twitched. I pressed before I read the flag. The pair left without me in one direction and with my money in the other. The screen stayed pretty. The wallet took a minus the confetti does not draw.

Then I did what I did on the research desk and the seven-agent ring. I took away the right to press. I left the right to look.

Chief is not a DJ anymore. Dispatch. Routing: WHALE, EXIT, SHILL, SEARCH, RUG, RISK. Not “buy.” “Here is where to look. Here is where it smells.” Sniper does not fire. It drops a card: pair, liquidity, who is on top, whether the pool is burned. Rug is not a hero. A guard. If a thread drops, LP is unlocked, a whale is leaving, the desk writes three lines and shuts up. Shill does not post in someone else’s chat. It writes to me: this looks like heat, not a product.

You cannot live on that if you confuse the chart with the till.

+134 SOL on the panel is set dressing. Real money showed up when I stopped selling “I catch pairs.” I started selling a morning without panic. Two or three people who cannot sit in the feed. By morning, a stack: what is alive, what is already dead, where the whale is, where the shill is, where you should not put a hand. Forty minutes to decide what from the stack is not shameful to send. I do not press PUMP for them. Or for me.

The first decent month was ugly again. Subscription. Tokens. One run where scan went too wide and dragged in junk. After costs, about three thousand was left. Rent. Food. The habit of not opening a chart before I read risk. The second month repeated. The easy life was dull again. Not a yacht from DOGY. A balance that does not jump off one green candle.

Where I almost burned it matters more than the pixels.

Shared machine. Let sniper near a wallet and rug is already in the same cookies. Fine for notes. Not fine for keys.

A pretty day PnL is not a paycheck. While you watch the confetti, the till drips fees, slippage, and one stupid button.

A swarm does not cancel greed. If the offer is “I’ll press for you,” seven agents just do the stupid thing faster. I saw it on myself. More flags. No more sense, until I took my finger off.

What’s left if you kill the neon.

I did not buy freedom with a Ridark desk. I bought a night shift that sorts someone else’s noise into boxes by morning: whale, shill, rug, risk. Then I spend forty minutes deciding what’s alive in the boxes. And I get the day a feed with twenty tickers used to eat.

People watch the clip for pixels and a PUMP button. You live on other math: narrow permissions, a stop before any trade, three clients for a quiet Monday, and the habit of reading a flag before it becomes a minus.

Late evening it goes back to ROUTING — SEARCH. The desk is quiet. The core is white. I close the lid.

A quiet life does not start when the panel screams +203. It starts when morning is not ashamed of your finger.
